source.title: Scaling description of generalization with number of parameters in deep learning
source.authors: M. Geiger; Arthur Jacot; Stefano Spigler; Franck Gabriel; Levent Sagun; Stéphane d'Ascoli; G. Biroli; Clément Hongler; M. Wyart

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present, including supplementary materials.
record.tranche_reason: The paper sweeps parameter count and measures training and test error, including behavior around the jamming transition and beyond it. This conceptually tests width-dependent generalization, but its fully connected MNIST setup uses parity labels and a selected PCA representation, and its CNN results measure filter-count changes and ensembling.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own parameter-count sweeps and training/test results. It does not test random-label memorization, architecture comparisons against fully connected networks on the same image setup, optimizer comparisons, batch-size effects, dropout, or memorized-example removal. Cited findings from other studies are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study directly measures training and held-out error while widening fixed-depth networks beyond their fitting threshold. Its deeper ReLU networks, MNIST parity task, and CIFAR-10 CNNs provide different-method tests of V2.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly correct. The authors empirically observe improving individual-network generalization at large parameter counts and propose a heuristic NTK explanation through diminishing output fluctuations. They explain the threshold spike through an apparent output-norm divergence and suggest ensembling moderately beyond the threshold for computational efficiency. They explicitly say this practical recommendation needs testing across more architectures and datasets.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies parameter-count sweeps using a theoretical NTK framework and empirical MNIST/CIFAR10 experiments. Its fully connected models use ADAM with full-batch training; its CNNs use SGD. These experiments differ from the specific model and dataset recipes in V2.
record.method_sensitivity: Test error varies with parameter count and changes sharply near the jamming transition. Ensemble averaging changes reported CIFAR10 accuracy; CNN filter-count conditions and architecture differ from the fully connected MNIST sweep.

fits_no_version.finding: Twenty-model CIFAR-10 ensembles achieve approximately 80.5–80.7% accuracy near f≈40–64, with peak ensemble accuracy at f=64.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Averaging independently initialized networks moderately beyond the fitting threshold can outperform individual much wider networks.

fits_no_version.finding: On MNIST, averaging 20 independently initialized networks makes post-threshold test error nearly flat; moderately sized ensembles can perform slightly better than very wide ensembles.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The benefit of widening individual networks can diminish or reverse after output averaging removes initialization variance.

record.peer_reviewed: Journal of Statistical Mechanics: Theory and Experiment
record.problems: The fully connected MNIST experiment uses parity classification on only the first 10 PCA components, not the specified natural-label benchmark setup. The CNN filter-count description does not provide numerical results for every filter count, and the evidence does not establish monotonic test-error improvement across width. The paper describes some scaling arguments as heuristic rather than proofs.
record.rows_left_out: No additional qualifying results identified. Ensemble accuracy is retained as a separate result because the paper reports it separately and it changes the performance condition.

untested.parts: No paired natural-label and fixed-random-label training and held-out results.
The original one-hidden-layer recipe and downsampled CIFAR-10 experiment are not replicated; the fully connected experiment uses deeper networks and PCA-reduced MNIST parity classification.
No controlled convolutional versus fully connected comparison or test of the stated connectivity and initialization mechanisms.
No optimizer comparison under matched workloads and tuning budgets.
No batch-size comparison under fixed epoch budgets.
No magnitude-aware weight-perturbation sharpness measure or ranking of generalization gaps.
No removal and retraining comparison involving memorized examples.

record.verdict_notes: This study is not an original source for V2, so verdicts are appropriate. Differences from the original architecture and task establish the tested setting; they are not themselves evidence against V2. The CNN source contains an apparent performance/error wording inconsistency, so its slight deterioration at the widest sizes warrants a scope qualification rather than a strong challenge.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label generalization coexistence; random-label chance performance; the specified Inception, AlexNet and MLP experiments.

The exact one-hidden-layer ReLU setup and the specified MNIST and downsampled CIFAR-10 experiments; the paper tests fixed-depth fully connected networks on PCA-reduced MNIST parity labels and a CNN filter-count sweep on CIFAR-10.
A controlled convolutional versus fully connected comparison, local connectivity's contribution, learned sparse connections, and convolutional initialization.
Comparative adaptive versus non-adaptive optimizer results and the specified tuning, decay, switching, and language-model conditions.
Large versus small batch comparisons under fixed epoch budgets and the specified batch-size adaptations.
Dropout comparisons and the stated training-set-size, underfitting, augmentation, and weight-decay conditions.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its comparison with norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing memorized examples and comparing retraining accuracy with random-example removal.

rows.subject: fully-connected networks, depth L = 5
rows.stage_stated: trained to end of training; t = 2·106 epochs
rows.operation_detail: Sweep number of parameters N while training on MNIST parity classification using first 10 PCA components.

conditions.value: MNIST; P = 10k training images and 50k test images
fully-connected, depth L = 5, input dimension nin = 10
no regularization; early stopping shown separately

rows.measure: test error versus number of parameters
rows.value: test error reaches a local maximum in a cusp-like fashion near N ∗ and then slowly decreases as N becomes larger; the figure's fitted asymptote is ϵ∞ = 0.054
rows.note: The stated result is a cusp followed by a slow decrease, rather than monotonic decrease across the full sweep. Numerical asymptote and fit coefficients are reported for the fitted curve.
rows.check: The post-threshold test-error decline supports V2. The cusp at the fitting threshold does not make this effect partial: V2 concerns widening beyond that threshold. Training lasts at most 2 million full-batch steps and stops when loss reaches zero; the fitted 0.054 asymptote is not a directly observed limiting error.

rows.subject: CNN, three convolutional and one fully-connected layer
rows.size_stated: filter count f varies from 21 to 211
rows.stage_stated: trained on CIFAR10; n = 20 models for each f
rows.operation_detail: Sweep convolutional filter count f, measuring average test performance across independently initialized models.

conditions.value: 3 convolutional and 1 fully-connected layers; output is 10-dimensional
no momentum, weight decay, or data augmentation

rows.value: Soon after the transition, at f ∼ 40, 48, 64, mean performances are ∼ 67–72%; the widest models' average accuracy is a little less than ∼ 77.5%; average performance without ensembling is lowest at f = 1280 with a value of ∼ 77.5%.
rows.note: The reported mean-accuracy descriptions do not establish a monotonic test-error decrease as width increases; f is the CNN filter count, not the V2 one-hidden-layer width.
rows.check: Accuracy improves substantially beyond the transition, from approximately 67–72% at f≈40–64 to approximately 77.5% at f=1280, but the widest models perform slightly worse. The source's description of the lowest average performance at f=1280 conflicts with its accuracy values and error plot; this should be identified as an apparent wording error, with minimum error intended. The filter range is 2^1 to 2^11, not 21 to 211. Learning rate also varies across widths as 1/f.

source_check.locator_found: Section 8, paragraph preceding Figure 8; Figure 8 caption; Materials and methods.

rows.subject: CNN ensemble of n = 20 independently initialized models
rows.operation_detail: Sweep filter count and average outputs across 20 independently initialized models.
rows.value: ensemble performance is ∼ 80.5–80.7%; peak performance is achieved by ensembling with f = 64, yielding ∼ 80.7%.
rows.note: Ensembling is part of the reported condition and affects the performance; these results do not isolate the V2 claim about an individual network's width beyond its interpolation threshold.
rows.check: These values measure accuracy after averaging outputs from 20 networks. They do not establish how an individual network's test error changes beyond its fitting threshold.

rows.subject: fully-connected networks, depth L = 5
rows.stage_stated: trained to end of training; t = 2·106 epochs
rows.operation_detail: Sweep number of parameters N while training on MNIST parity classification using first 10 PCA components.

conditions.value: fully-connected, depth L = 5, input dimension nin = 10

rows.measure: training error versus number of parameters
rows.value: Training error reaches its minimum around the jamming transition; Figure 2(B) plots training error versus N.
rows.note: The text describes the minimum training loss at the end of training and specifies that the training error reaches its global minimum above N ∗.
rows.check: This is supporting evidence locating the fitting threshold for R1, not an independent measurement of generalization. Specify that the square-hinge training loss reaches zero above N*=825, implying zero classification error. Training loss and classification error should not be conflated.
